candidates.label: Shechem (Tell Balata)
candidates.support: Some scholarship treats Sychar as a variant name for the ancient city of Shechem, whose remains lie at Tell Balata; OpenBible.info's ancient-place catalog records this identification as an alternative for Sychar's ancient-name resolution.

unmappedCandidates.label: Askar
unmappedCandidates.support: The modern village of Askar, near Jacob's well on the lower slope of Mount Ebal, is proposed in Bible-geography scholarship as Sychar's modern equivalent; OpenBible.info's ancient-place catalog records this identification with a higher aggregate confidence (65%) than the Shechem/Tell Balata alternative (25%), based on the reference works it surveys. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) discusses the proposal and notes two difficulties: the initial ʿain in the modern name, a change from 'Sychar' the encyclopedia calls unusual but not impossible; and the presence of Askar's own spring, which would have made it unnecessary for the village's residents to fetch water from Jacob's well, a difficulty the encyclopedia judges would probably by itself be fatal to Askar's claim.
unmappedCandidates.reason: No coordinate for the village of Askar could be confirmed against an accepted source; the nearest confirmed independent point, the Askar refugee camp, sits roughly 800 m away and describes a different feature.

summary.text: Sychar is the Samaritan town where, according to John's Gospel, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. Its precise location is debated: some identify it with the modern village of Askar, others with the ancient city of Shechem at nearby Tell Balata. Only the Shechem/Tell Balata candidate is on the map; Askar is listed with the proposed sites but has no map point.

scripture.textWEB: So he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.

otConnections.note: John 4:5 explicitly recalls this plot of ground near Shechem that Jacob gave to his son Joseph, tying the Gospel scene to the patriarchal narrative.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
